item.title: Maestro splits in two, MCP goes stateless, and an e-invoice deadline lands
item.description: Issue one: the architectural split behind UiPath FUSION, Gartner’s warning on vendor-built agents, the new MCP spec, the EU AI Act calendar, Türkiye’s 1 January 2027 e-Arşiv rule and IXP’s new pricing unit.
item.content:encoded:
As this is the first issue, the window is wider than a week. Six items from recent weeks that could change the budget, the architecture or the calendar of an automation programme. They share a thread: as the tools mature, the question moves from “can it do this?” to “who will own it, and what will it cost?”

UiPath FUSION 2026: Maestro is now two products

UiPath · 23 September 2026

At FUSION 2026 UiPath split Maestro in two. Maestro Orchestrate is for long-running processes that cross teams and systems; Maestro Automate is for small, fast, high-volume tasks. Several things went generally available in the same announcement: Cartographer, which drafts and maintains a “Map of Work” from documents, systems and people; UiPath for Coding Agents, which lets developers build with the coding agent they already use; and Delegate, a desktop agent. Dark Testing Factory is in preview and the Map of Work itself is on the roadmap.

Why it matters. The split turns a decision teams already make into a product boundary. A case that stays open for weeks waiting on human approval and a queue item that finishes in seconds shouldn’t be governed by the same rules. Make that distinction in your architecture documents now: which processes hold state, and which only carry volume? I’d treat Cartographer as a way to keep the PDD current, not as a replacement for writing one. My first test would be a small process that already has documentation, comparing the output against what’s on file.

Gartner: most vendor-built agents will be abandoned

Gartner · 29 September 2026

Gartner’s 29 September release predicts that 70% of enterprises will abandon agentic AI built by a vendor’s forward-deployed engineers by 2028. The published summary points to rising costs and to organisations being unable to evolve these systems on their own. Gartner’s page blocks automated access, so this item rests on the release title and its published summary.

Why it matters. Outsourcing an agent build isn’t the problem. Being unable to maintain what you received is. I would put three things in the contract: versioned prompts and tool definitions, the evaluation sets used in acceptance testing, and at least one change made by the internal team alone after go-live. If the third can’t happen, what you have is a dependency, not a product.

Model Context Protocol 2026-07-28: the protocol is now stateless

Model Context Protocol Blog · 28 July 2026

The 28 July release moves MCP’s core to a stateless request-response model. The initialisation handshake and session IDs are gone; each request carries its own version and capability information. When a server needs input mid-call it now uses Multi Round-Trip Requests, and method and tool names travel in HTTP headers (Mcp-Method, Mcp-Name). Authorisation was tightened, and Tasks, MCP Apps and Enterprise Managed Authorization became official extensions. Roots, Sampling and Logging are deprecated, with at least twelve months to migrate.

Why it matters. If you run MCP servers in-house there is good news on two fronts. Servers scale horizontally without sticky sessions, and a gateway can see which tool is being called and apply policy without opening the request body. That gives you something concrete to discuss with the security team. The work is clear too: list which of your servers use the deprecated features now. Twelve months is short if you don’t have an inventory.

EU AI Act: high-risk delayed, transparency not

Official Journal of the European Union · 24 July 2026

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, entered into force on 27 July, three days after publication. Obligations for high-risk systems under Annex III move to 2 December 2027, and those for systems embedded in products under Annex I to 2 August 2028. The Article 50 transparency duties did not move; telling people they are dealing with an AI system has applied since 2 August 2026. Providers whose generative systems were on the market before that date get a four-month transition for machine-readable marking of outputs, which ends on 2 December 2026.

Why it matters. For Turkish companies serving the EU, or with EU customers, the order of work has changed. There’s breathing room on high-risk classification, but if a chatbot talks to customers or a flow generates text for them, the disclosure duty is current. I’d start with an inventory: in which flows is a person corresponding with a model without knowing it?

Türkiye e-Arşiv: the last quarter for small taxpayers

TÜRMOB · 2 January 2026 (Official Gazette, 31 December 2025)

General Communiqué No. 589 on the Tax Procedure Law gave taxpayers on the simplified method or business-account basis, who are outside e-Fatura and e-Arşiv, one extra year. Until 31 December 2026 they may issue invoices up to 3,000 TL including taxes on paper; anything above must be issued as e-Arşiv through the GİB portal. From 1 January 2027 every invoice they issue, whatever the amount, must be e-Arşiv. For other taxpayers the same rule has applied since 1 January 2026.

Why it matters. Companies that buy from many small suppliers still see paper or scanned invoices in accounts payable. Expect that channel to shrink in 2027. If you run an OCR flow for paper invoices, redo next year’s volume forecast with this change in mind. I’d move the freed capacity to integrations that take e-document data straight into the ERP.

IXP: priced per operation, not per page

UiPath Documentation · 8 July and 14 September 2026

Since 8 July, UiPath meters IXP extraction from unstructured and complex documents per operation rather than at a flat rate per page, and IXP and Document Understanding licences can be used together without extra per-page cost. On 23 July an option to deploy a model version straight to an Orchestrator folder entered preview. On 14 September Bring Your Own Subscription opened in preview: IXP can run on an organisation’s own Gemini or GPT subscription, eligible projects get discounted consumption, and AI Trust Layer policies still apply.

Why it matters. Document-processing business cases are usually built on page counts. Change the unit and the maths changes, and only your own sample will show which document types it helps and which it hurts. Re-run the business case on a real month of documents. For organisations that already hold a model subscription, BYOS adds an option in conversations about data residency and price. It’s still a preview, though.

Over the coming weeks I’ll be watching two things: availability dates for Maestro Orchestrate and Automate, and what model providers publish as the 2 December marking date approaches.

item.title: Catching anomalies in logistics: rules, a model and a person in one flow
item.description: The logistics anomaly detection we built with UiPath Maestro and agents: rule-based checks, classification with a language model and automatic notification to operations, plus the reasoning behind that division of labour.
item.content:encoded:
Logistics data is a tempting place to ask a language model, “anything odd in these records?” The records are messy, description fields are free text, and the exceptions keep changing. Ask the model that question directly, though, and you lose two things: consistency and control over cost.

The logistics anomaly flow we built with UiPath Maestro and agents splits the work three ways: rule-based RPA checks, classification with a language model, and automatic exception notification to operations stakeholders. This piece is about the reasoning behind that split.

How a shipment record moves through the flow

Rules, classification and notification are the backbone of the flow we delivered. The detail inside each step, and the human review gate, are the design I recommend for flows like this.

System

Data pull

Shipment records are pulled from the source systems at set intervals and brought into one format. Every later step works on that shared shape.

Rule

Rule checks

Deterministic checks run first: missing fields, thresholds exceeded, duplicate records and the like. There’s no point asking a model something a rule can answer with certainty.

Model

Classification

Records the rules flagged go to a language model together with their description and note fields. The model returns an anomaly type and a short rationale against a predefined schema.

Rule

Routing

The path splits on type and on the model’s confidence. Clear cases go straight to notification; uncertain ones go to human review.

Human

Human review

For uncertain cases an operations owner makes the call and records it with a reason. Those records are the best data you’ll get on where the model struggles.

System

Notify and audit

The right stakeholder is notified automatically, and the record, decision and rationale go to the audit trail. The same anomaly shouldn’t trigger a second message unless its status changes.

1 / 6

Don’t ask the model what a rule already knows

If a mandatory field on a shipment record is empty, you don’t need a language model to say so. Same if a defined threshold is exceeded or the same record arrives twice. These checks are cheap, give the same answer every time, and are easy to explain in an audit.

The model belongs where a rule can’t decide on its own. Free text is the clearest case, I think. The reason for a delay buried in an operations note, a phrase in a description field, what an inconsistency between two fields actually means: these are hard to capture with rules, and every new situation adds another rule. That’s where classification earns its place.

The ordering has a side benefit. The model only sees records the rules flagged, so cost grows with the number of suspicious records rather than the total.

Ask the model for a form, not an essay

Binding the model’s output to a predefined schema is what keeps the rest of the flow solid. The anomaly type should come from a fixed list, the rationale should be short, and there should be a field where the model can say it isn’t sure. A model that returns free text forces every later step to guess.

Writing the list of types with the operations team is part of the job. When something new shows up that isn’t on the list, a model that marks it as “other” is better than one that forces it into the wrong bucket.

Notification is design work too

Automatic notification can be the least discussed and most complained-about part of a flow. If everyone gets everything, soon nobody reads anything. When I design notifications I look at three things:

  • Who receives it? The team or person responsible for that anomaly type.
  • What do they see? The record, the anomaly type and a one-line rationale. Nobody should have to log in and search.
  • When do they hear about it again? Not for the same anomaly, unless its status changes.

Where Maestro fits

Orchestration here means running the steps in the right order and making visible which stage a record is waiting in. Rule, model and human steps move at very different speeds: a rule finishes in milliseconds, a human review can take hours. UiPath splitting Maestro at FUSION 2026 into Orchestrate for long-running processes and Automate for short high-volume work recognises that difference at the product level. I went into it a little more in the first radar.

Put the human gate in from the start

The core of the flow we delivered is rules, classification and notification. If I built a similar flow again, I’d add a human review step for cases where the model isn’t sure from day one. My reason is simple: those records are the most valuable data you’ll get on which anomaly types trip the model up. When the human decision is recorded with a reason, the next improvement knows where to start.

Measure before you scale

Before rolling an anomaly flow out to a new region or a new data source, I’d measure three things:

  1. Classification accuracy on a small labelled sample. Write it into acceptance testing.
  2. The false-alarm rate. The operations team’s trust is won or lost in the first few weeks.
  3. Cost per record. Model calls grow with volume; rule checks don’t.

If none of the three is measured, you have a promising demo. That’s all.

item.title: Reading an invoice is not understanding it: on-prem document processing at an airline
item.description: The document-processing line we built for the finance team of a national flag carrier, running in the airline’s own data centre. Multi-language, multi-currency invoices, human validation and the decisions that shaped the design.
item.content:encoded:
Reading the text on an invoice is no longer hard. OCR engines have done it well for years. The hard part is understanding what was read. Which amount is the total and which is a line? Which date is the invoice date and which is the due date? Is the table on page two a continuation of page one, or a separate breakdown?

The document-processing programme we built for the Finance and Accounting function of a national flag carrier is built on that second question. It runs in the airline’s own data centre, processes supplier invoices end to end, and is live. Without going into the airline’s internal details, this piece walks through the decisions that shaped the design.

How a supplier invoice moves through the line

The skeleton of the flow. I’m not sharing the airline’s internal details or volumes; the steps show how a programme like this is put together. Click a step, or press play.

System

Intake

Whatever channel an invoice arrives through (email, scan, portal), it lands in a single intake queue. Each document gets a traceable ID, and a second copy of the same invoice is caught here.

Model

Digitisation

OCR/ICR turns the page into text with positions. The installation runs in the airline’s own data centre, so the document never leaves the building at any stage.

Model

Classification

The document type and language are identified. An invoice, a delivery note and attachments can arrive in one file; extraction only means something once the type is right.

Model

Extraction

Header fields (supplier, date, due date, currency) and line-item tables are extracted. Several tables, tables split across pages and country-specific decimal formats are handled here.

Rule

Rule checks

Do the lines add up to the invoice total? Does the currency fit the supplier? Is the supplier in master data? Each field’s confidence score is compared with the threshold set for that field.

Human

Human validation

A document below threshold, or one that fails a rule, goes to the validation screen. The reviewer doesn’t reread the whole invoice; they see the field that stopped and why.

System

Posting and audit

Approved data is posted to the ERP. Who corrected what is written to the audit trail, and corrected fields become input for the next model improvement.

1 / 7

The first constraint: documents don’t leave the building

The first decision that shaped the architecture wasn’t technical. It was institutional: documents would not be sent outside the organisation. That’s a common requirement for finance documents and, I think, a fair one. A supplier invoice carries bank details, contract prices and payment terms.

The consequence is that much of what you switch on with a few settings in the cloud becomes infrastructure work on-premises. Digitisation and extraction components have to run inside. Model versions, updates and capacity planning become part of the project. UiPath’s own documentation states that Document Understanding remains available for Automation Suite and Standalone deployments, which narrows the choice of product for any organisation with an on-premises requirement.

The lesson here, as I see it, is simple: plan the on-premises installation as its own work item, not a deployment detail. If it isn’t in the schedule from day one, it will squeeze something later.

Three gaps between reading and understanding

The scope of this programme fits in three phrases: multi-currency, multi-language, multi-table. Each is its own problem.

Multiple currencies. The currency isn’t always printed next to the amount. Decimal separators change from country to country, and the same supplier can change format over time. After extraction every amount has to be normalised and its currency checked against what the supplier usually invoices in. I’d leave that check to a rule, not the model. The model can be wrong; the fact that a supplier always bills in euros is already sitting in master data.

Multiple languages. The same field arrives under different labels in different languages, and non-Latin scripts are a challenge of their own. On another project we built a separate extraction pipeline for documents in Chinese characters, and it raised accuracy by 55%. That result points at something: instead of forcing every language through one model, splitting the troublesome language into its own pipeline is worth trying.

Multiple tables. Line items can be spread across several tables, tables break at the end of a page, and subtotals can look like lines. The best insurance is, again, a rule: if the lines don’t add up to the invoice total, the document doesn’t pass automatically.

Human validation is the design, not the fallback

Two parts of this programme set it apart: the design of the validation screen, and structured human-in-the-loop escalation. The second sounds abstract, so let me unpack it.

In unstructured escalation, a document goes to a person with a note that says “please check”. They reread it, find the problem themselves and repeat the same work every time. In structured escalation the document arrives with the reason it stopped: which field, which rule, which confidence score. Documents that stop for different reasons can go to different people. An unreadable field is work for the validation team; a supplier missing from master data is work for procurement.

There are two benefits. The reviewer’s time goes to the suspicious field, not the whole document. And because corrections are recorded with their reasons, you can measure which document types and which fields cause trouble. Those records decide where model improvement starts.

I set confidence thresholds per field, not per document. A small misread in the supplier name gets caught by master-data matching; a misread amount can turn into a payment before anyone notices. Applying the same threshold to both makes little sense.

Before you copy this

If a team were starting a similar programme, this is the list I’d hand them:

  1. Collect a real month of documents. Don’t estimate anything before you’ve seen the spread of suppliers, languages, currencies and page counts.
  2. Write down who will work the validation screen and how much time they have each week. A human step without capacity becomes a queue that slows everything down.
  3. Decide with the business which field passes at which threshold, and name the owner of that decision.
  4. Define the final consistency checks before posting to the ERP as rules. However good the model is, don’t leave those to it.
  5. If you’re on-premises, put hardware, OCR engine licensing and the model-update procedure in the plan as separate lines.
  6. Have a rollback plan for model version changes. A new version can improve one field and get worse on another.

None of these items is about AI. Most of the decisions that decide a document-processing project aren’t.

item.title: Document Understanding or IXP? A decision table by document type
item.description: A practical guide to choosing between UiPath’s two document-AI routes, starting from the document type, your generative-AI policy and where the system has to run. Grounded in UiPath’s own documentation.
item.content:encoded:
UiPath now has two routes for documents, and the choice often starts in the wrong place: with “which one is newer?” A better starting point is the document itself. Two questions follow. How much generative AI does your organisation allow, and where will the system run?

At BOTTEQ we build document-processing lines by combining Document Understanding with Base64.ai’s OCR/ICR engines. The table below doesn’t come from that work, though. It comes from UiPath’s own documentation, with the sources at the end. The commentary is mine.

The two routes in brief

Document Understanding (DU) is for structured and semi-structured documents: forms, purchase orders, applications, invoices. It works with pre-trained machine-learning models on documents whose layout is the same or very close. Its generative features can be governed through the organisation’s AI Trust Layer policies. DU continues as a standalone service and remains available on Automation Suite and Standalone deployments.

IXP is the umbrella under which UiPath brought DU and Communications Mining together and added a new prompt-driven capability: generative extraction for unstructured and complex documents. UiPath describes it for annual reports, contracts and lease agreements. Complex tables, charts, checkboxes, signatures and handwriting, values that have to be inferred from context or stitched together across sections: that’s this route’s territory. Generative AI is mandatory here.

Decision table

SituationMy recommendationBasis
Forms, orders, applications, invoices with a largely fixed layoutDocument UnderstandingUiPath describes these as DU’s territory
Contracts, leases, annual reports; values inferred from contextIXP, generative extractionComplex structure, contextual inference and cross-section stitching are what this route is described for
Emails, workflow tickets, short messagesIXP, Communications MiningBuilt for short, free-text communication
The organisation restricts generative AIDocument UnderstandingGenerative features can be governed here; they’re mandatory in IXP’s generative extraction
Documents can’t leave the organisationDocument UnderstandingDU continues on Automation Suite and Standalone; confirm IXP availability for your own deployment
Long, multi-page filesCheck page limits firstThe documented limit for generative extraction is 50 pages, up to 150 in preview; up to 500 with DU activities

Three questions the table can’t answer

Mixed bundles. When ID, proof of address and bank statements arrive in a single file, as with a loan application, the real work starts before extraction: splitting the documents and identifying their types. Whichever route you pick, settle where and how that splitting happens during the pilot. The division of labour between rules, a model and a person here can matter more than the extraction itself.

Project type. DU has a choice inside it too. Modern projects give faster, guided model development. Classic projects allow exporting models and datasets and cross-tenant use, but run only on Automation Cloud. AI Center-based projects give the most control and also support Standalone deployments, but have no Cloud API support. If you must run on-premises, that alone can decide the matter.

The cost unit. Since July 2026, IXP extraction from unstructured and complex documents is metered per operation rather than at a flat rate per page, and IXP and DU licences can be used together without extra per-page cost. If you have an old business case built on page counts, re-run it on a real sample of documents.

Two traps when moving to IXP

The label you confirm is what counts as right. IXP scores a model against the labels you confirmed. Confirm a wrong value while labelling and it becomes the reference, and the score goes up. A high score doesn’t prove the values are correct. Treat labelling as part of acceptance testing, not a chore to finish quickly.

Don’t mistake a format difference for an error. Built-in data types such as dates and monetary amounts come back normalised. If “21-JUN-22” on the page and the ISO date the model returns are the same value, that isn’t a mistake. What deserves your attention is a change in meaning, such as a misread decimal separator.

My default

If most of the document set is invoices, forms or orders with a known layout, I start with Document Understanding. I gather the documents that take the most validation time, the ones with scattered layouts or values that depend on context, into a separate queue, and I try IXP on that queue first. The two routes can run side by side in the same line. I think it’s healthier to treat the choice as a decision per document type than as a one-off platform decision.

item.title: Seven questions before you give an agent decision rights
item.description: Most agentic projects stall over ownership, cost and risk control rather than technology. Seven questions I ask before go-live, with Türkiye’s KVKK guidance on agentic AI and the EU rules taken into account.
item.content:encoded:
In June 2025 Gartner predicted that over 40% of agentic AI projects would be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Model quality isn’t on that list. Agents mostly stall not because they can’t do the work, but because nobody is sure what they’re doing or what it costs.

We’ve built change-management, monitoring and incident-response frameworks inside client organisations, and at the heart of that work is a plain fact: putting a system live means giving it authority. For RPA bots that authority was narrow; a bot followed steps someone had written down. An agent picks its own next step. So the questions you ask before signing off go-live change too. Here are mine.

1. Does it decide, or recommend?

The same agent carries very different risk in the two roles. An agent that classifies a supply anomaly and puts it in front of a person is recommending. An agent that lifts a payment block on its own is deciding. Write this down for every action in the design document. “The agent does X” isn’t enough; say “the agent proposes X and this person approves” or “the agent does X and stops in this situation”.

2. Can a wrong decision be undone, and what does it cost?

I suggest ranking actions on two axes: can it be reversed, and what does a mistake cost? Reversible, cheap actions can be left to the agent. Irreversible or expensive ones need a human approval gate. That gate isn’t an admission that the agent falls short; it’s a deliberate split of authority. Where the gate sits can change over time, too. As the records show the agent is reliable on a given type of action, you can pull the gate back.

3. Which tools can it reach, and under which identity?

Every tool an agent can call is a list of everything it can do. An agent running with a human user’s permissions can make every mistake that user could. You need a separate service identity, only the tools it needs, and the narrowest permissions that work. The July 2026 release of the Model Context Protocol helps here: method and tool names now travel in HTTP headers, so a gateway can see which tool is being called and apply policy without opening the request body.

4. Did you define “correct” before writing the agent?

An agent project without acceptance criteria is a demo that never ends. Before writing the agent, build a small evaluation set from real examples: for this input, which output is right, which is acceptable, which is wrong? That set becomes the basis for acceptance testing and for regression testing after every prompt change. On outsourced projects it belongs on the list of deliverables.

5. Does every run leave a trace?

When an agent does something wrong, the first question is “why?” To answer it you need, for every run, a record of the input, the tools called, what they returned, the model’s output and the cost. Those records are the raw material of incident response; without them every investigation is guesswork. There’s a second benefit: the trace shows what each task costs, which makes the budget conversation concrete.

6. Does it touch personal data?

On 12 March 2026 Türkiye’s data protection authority, KVKK, published guidance on agentic AI systems. According to the legal summaries, it expects organisations to have a data-governance framework and risk assessment covering their use of agentic AI, clear responsibilities between the parties processing data, human oversight designed in from the start, privacy by design and by default, and staff who understand what these systems do with data. Each of those maps onto one of the questions above. If your agent processes personal data, write that mapping down. It’s the first document an auditor will ask for.

If you serve the EU there’s one more item. The AI Act’s transparency obligations were not postponed by the new regulation. An agent that corresponds directly with people has to tell them they are dealing with an AI system.

7. What happens when you switch it off?

This is the question asked least. When the agent fails, when its cost jumps unexpectedly, or when the model provider changes something, who takes over the work? I expect every agent to have a written fallback: if a rule-based robot can do the same job, that robot should be on standby; if not, the work should drop into a human queue. Who holds the off switch, and which signal triggers the decision to use it, should be written down as well.

If the answer is “we don’t know”

If the answer to any of these seven is “we don’t know”, you aren’t running an agent in production. You’re running a pilot in production. That’s fine, as long as everyone knows it’s a pilot. The trouble starts on the day a pilot is budgeted like a product and audited like one.
